title: Monitoring (Advanced): Log Analytics, KQL and Application Insights
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Design a Log Analytics workspace: how many, where, who can read what, how long data stays, and which table plan each table needs.
- Choose the right collection pipe — diagnostic settings, the Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules, or Application Insights — for each kind of data.
- Write KQL queries with where, project, summarize, bin, render and join, and turn a query into a log search alert.
- Use Application Insights — OpenTelemetry, requests, dependencies, failures, availability tests and the application map — to find where the time goes.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

The alerts from Lunch 16 work. Last Friday the CPU alert stayed quiet — no server passed 50% CPU — yet checkout took four seconds, and the payments team counted 312 abandoned carts between 19:00 and 20:00.

On Monday everyone has a theory. Dewi blames the product images in Blob storage. Pak Budi blames the VM that runs the order jobs. Rizky, the contractor, blames the payment provider. Each of them opens a different screen, and none of the screens agree.

Ibu Sari asks the question that matters: "Why was checkout slow on Friday — and will it happen again on 12.12?" Harbolnas, the national online-shopping day, is less than two months away.

Today you put all the evidence in one place, learn the language to question it, and turn the answer into an alert.

Reading

1. Design the workspace before you collect anything

A Log Analytics workspace is a regional Azure resource that stores log data in tables. Agent data, resource logs, the exported activity log and Application Insights telemetry all land in tables there, and every table has a schema, a retention period and a price. Because moving data between workspaces later is painful, a few design decisions belong at the start.

How many workspaces? As few as you can justify. One workspace makes cross-source questions easy: a single query can line up application requests with VM counters and storage logs. Split only for a real reason:

- Data residency — Nusantara Retail's customer data must stay in Indonesia Central, so production logs that may contain customer details go to a workspace there.
- Different owners — a security team running Microsoft Sentinel often wants its own workspace and access rules.
- Billing or scale — separate cost centres, or very large volumes with their own pricing commitments.

When you do split, the workspace() function lets one query read several workspaces.

Who can read what? With resource-context access, anyone who can read a resource can query that resource's logs without being given the whole workspace. Workspace-context access is for operators who need everything, and table-level permissions protect sensitive tables.

How long is data kept? A table on the Analytics plan has an analytics retention — 30 days by default (90 days for Application Insights tables and Sentinel-enabled workspaces), extendable to two years — during which it's fully queryable. Every table, whatever its plan, also has a total retention of up to 12 years. Data past the analytics retention moves to cheap long-term retention, which you reach with search jobs or by restoring it. The default retention is included in the ingestion price; you pay extra only for keeping data longer.

Which table plan? Every table has a plan that trades query power for price. (The current docs label the third plan Auxiliary / Lake.)

| Analytics | Basic | Auxiliary
Best for | data you alert on and query every day | troubleshooting and incident data | verbose, rarely read logs kept for audit
Which tables | all | selected Azure tables and custom tables | selected Azure tables and custom tables
Ingestion price | standard | reduced | minimal
Query price | included | charged per GB scanned | charged per GB scanned
Query speed | fast | fast | slower
Alerts | yes | simple log alerts only | no
Dashboards | everything, including insights | workbooks and Grafana | workbooks and Grafana, slow to refresh
Typical Nusantara table | AppRequests, Perf, Syslog | verbose container logs | audit logs kept for years

Section 5 returns to cost. For now, remember the rule behind every plan: the more often you need data quickly, the more you pay to store it.

2. Getting data in: three pipes

Nusantara Retail's Friday evidence lives in three places — the platform, the servers and the application — and each has its own pipe into the workspace.

Data | Pipe | Lands in | Remember
Resource logs: blob reads, Key Vault access, SQL audit | Diagnostic setting on the resource | resource-specific tables such as StorageBlobLogs (or the older shared AzureDiagnostics) | up to five settings per resource; use category groups such as allLogs
Activity log | Diagnostic setting on the subscription | AzureActivity | free to ingest
Guest OS: Syslog, Windows events, performance counters, text files | Azure Monitor Agent + data collection rule | Syslog, Event, Perf, custom _CL tables | needs a managed identity and an association
Application requests, dependencies, exceptions, logs | Application Insights | AppRequests, AppDependencies, AppExceptions, AppTraces | autoinstrumentation or OpenTelemetry
Your own records | Logs ingestion API + data collection rule | custom _CL tables | you define the schema

Diagnostic settings route a resource's platform logs — and optionally its metrics — to a workspace, a storage account, Event Hubs or a partner solution. Prefer resource-specific tables, which have a proper schema per service, over the shared AzureDiagnostics table. One quirk surprises people: a diagnostic setting outlives its resource. If you delete a resource and later recreate one with the same name, the old setting can come back with it, so delete settings when you delete or rename resources. At scale, Azure Policy creates diagnostic settings for you (Lunch 31).

The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) is the only supported agent for collecting data from inside Windows and Linux machines, in Azure and — through Azure Arc — elsewhere. The legacy Log Analytics agent (also called MMA or OMS) was retired on August 31, 2024, and Microsoft warns that after March 2, 2026 its data uploads can stop at any time without notice; if you still find it on a server, migrating is urgent, not optional. AMA authenticates with the machine's managed identity (system-assigned is fine for a few machines; user-assigned scales better).

The agent does nothing until it receives a data collection rule (DCR). A DCR says three things:

1. What to collect — Syslog facilities with a minimum severity, performance counters with a sampling interval, Windows events filtered with XPath, or lines from text and JSON files.
2. How to shape it — an optional transformation, written in KQL, that drops rows or columns before they are stored.
3. Where to send it — one or more workspaces, or Azure Monitor Metrics.

A DCR association links a machine to a rule. The relationship is many-to-many: one "Linux baseline" DCR can serve every server, while the payment server also gets an extra rule for its application log. Installing the agent alone collects nothing — a classic first-day surprise.

VM insights packages this for you. When you enable monitoring for a VM in the portal today, the recommended metrics-based experience collects a default set of OpenTelemetry guest metrics into an Azure Monitor workspace (queried with PromQL, default metrics free), and the classic logs-based experience stores performance data in Log Analytics for KQL, workbooks and multi-VM views. You can use both.

Data isn't instant. Once a pipe is flowing, rows usually arrive within seconds to a few minutes. A brand-new agent, rule, diagnostic setting or table often needs 5–15 minutes before the first rows appear — plan your labs and your incident expectations accordingly.

Tip: Filter as early as possible. A DCR that collects Syslog at Warning and above sends a fraction of the data of one that collects Debug, and choosing only the counters you need beats collecting everything "just in case". You can't query what you didn't collect, but you pay for everything you do.

3. KQL: ask questions of your data

Kusto Query Language (KQL) is a read-only language. A query starts with a table and pipes the rows through operators, left to right, like a production line: each step receives rows and hands rows to the next. Three habits make queries fast and correct: start with the table, filter on time first, and only then filter, shape and aggregate. Table and column names are case-sensitive.

Operator | What it does | Example
where | keep matching rows | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
project | choose, rename or reorder columns | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SyslogMessage
extend | add a calculated column | extend Seconds = DurationMs / 1000.0
summarize | aggregate rows into groups | summarize count() by Computer
bin() | round values into buckets, usually time | summarize avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
percentile() | latency percentiles | summarize p95 = percentile(DurationMs, 95)
countif() | count rows that match a condition | summarize Failed = countif(Success == false)
arg_max() | the latest row per group | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by Computer
top, sort by | order rows | top 10 by DurationMs desc
render | draw a chart | render timechart
join | combine two tables on a key | join kind=leftouter (AppExceptions) on OperationId
union | stack tables | union AppTraces, AppExceptions
let | name a value or a subquery | let slow = 1000;
has, contains, =~ | text matching | where Name has "checkout"

Here is the query that started Nusantara Retail's investigation: the 95th-percentile duration of checkout requests in five-minute buckets.

AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-16 18:00) .. datetime(2026-10-16 21:00))
| where Name has "checkout"
| summarize p95 = percentile(DurationMs, 95), requests = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| render timechart

A few traps catch almost everyone:

- has versus contains. has matches whole terms and uses the index, so it's fast; contains matches any substring and is slower. == is case-sensitive; =~ isn't.
- The default join. Without kind=, a join is innerunique, which silently keeps only one row per key on the left side. Write kind=inner or kind=leftouter on purpose, and filter both sides before joining.
- Averages hide pain. An average checkout of 600 ms can hide one customer in twenty waiting four seconds. Use percentiles for latency.
- Scope. Opening Logs from a resource's menu scopes queries to that resource; open it from the workspace (or Monitor › Logs) to see everything. Log Analytics also has a point-and-click Simple mode beside KQL mode.

Queries on Analytics tables cost nothing extra; queries that touch Basic or Auxiliary tables are billed by the data they scan — one more reason to filter on time first.

4. Application Insights: see inside the code

Application Insights is Azure Monitor's application performance monitoring feature. Every Application Insights resource you create today is workspace-based: the telemetry lands in tables in a Log Analytics workspace, and the resource adds the portal experiences and the connection string your app uses to send data. Classic resources, which kept data separately, were retired in February 2024.

There are two ways to instrument an app:

- Autoinstrumentation — no code changes. On App Service you turn on Application Insights (two app settings when scripted) for .NET, Java, Node.js and, on Linux, Python; Azure Functions and AKS have their own options. Support differs per language and host, and some combinations are still in preview, so check the support table for yours.
- Code-based OpenTelemetry — you add Microsoft's OpenTelemetry distro to the app and initialise it at start-up. At the time of writing, new .NET, Node.js and Python apps use the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, and Java uses the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro (a Java agent). OpenTelemetry is an open standard, so the same instrumentation can also send to other backends. Sampling keeps volume and cost under control.

Telemetry | Table | Answers
Requests | AppRequests | Which pages and APIs were called, how long they took, and whether they failed
Dependencies | AppDependencies | Which outgoing calls — SQL, HTTP APIs, storage — were slow or failing
Exceptions | AppExceptions | What broke, with type, message and stack
Traces | AppTraces | What the code logged along the way
Availability results | AppAvailabilityResults | Whether the site answered from outside, from each test location
Page views and browser timings | AppPageViews, AppBrowserTimings | What real users experienced in the browser (needs the browser SDK)

Every row of one user action shares an operation ID, so you can follow a single checkout from the browser through the web app to the payment API and back. The portal turns this into views you'll use constantly:

- The application map draws components and their dependencies, with call rates, durations and failure rates.
- Performance and Failures list operations by duration or error count, show percentiles, and let you drill into one sample's end-to-end transaction.
- Live metrics stream request rates, failures and server health in near real time while you deploy or test. It isn't available with every instrumentation (for example, App Service autoinstrumentation for Python).
- Availability tests call a URL from Microsoft's test locations around the world. A standard test checks the status code, response time, content and TLS certificate validity; at least five locations are recommended, alerts fire when several locations fail, and standard tests are billed per run. The older URL ping tests were retired on September 30, 2026: create standard tests only.

5. From query to action — without breaking the bank

A log search alert runs a KQL query on a schedule. You choose a measurement (the number of rows, or an aggregated column such as average duration), optional dimensions to split the result — one alert per computer or per operation — a threshold, a frequency, a window (how far back each run looks) and how many violations must occur before it fires. Rules are stateful by default, so they resolve themselves when the condition clears, and they notify people through the same action groups as the metric alerts from Lunch 16. Each rule has a monthly cost that rises with the evaluation frequency, so five minutes is a sensible default. Two habits help:

- Write the query to describe the problem, not the alert. Return the slow requests and let the rule count them, and avoid take and limit, which make results inconsistent between runs.
- Allow for ingestion delay. An alert can only fire after its rows have arrived, so give the window comfortably more time than the delay you normally see.

For dashboards, workbooks combine parameters, queries, charts and text into interactive, shareable reports — the natural home for a "checkout health" page. Azure Monitor dashboards with Grafana add free, prebuilt Grafana dashboards inside the portal, and Azure Managed Grafana is the paid option for teams that also need non-Azure data sources and the full Grafana feature set. Business reports can go to Power BI. For charts over long periods, summary rules pre-aggregate raw data into a small table so dashboards stay fast.

Logs are usually the largest line on a monitoring bill, and they grow quietly as teams add sources. Analytics ingestion is billed per GB — at the time of writing the first 5 GB per billing account per month are free on pay-as-you-go — and some tables, including Heartbeat, AzureActivity and Usage, are free to ingest. These levers keep the rest under control:

Lever | What it does | Watch out for
Collect less | DCR severity levels, fewer counters, longer sampling intervals, Application Insights sampling | you can't query what you never collected
Transform at ingestion | a KQL transformation in the DCR drops noisy rows or columns before they're stored | dropping more than half of the incoming data adds a processing charge for the excess
Choose table plans | Basic or Auxiliary for verbose data you rarely query | queries are billed by data scanned; alerts are limited
Right-size retention | keep analytics retention short and older data in long-term retention | search jobs and restores have their own charges
Commitment tiers | a discount for steady Analytics volume from 100 GB per day | you pay for the tier even on quiet days
Watch the Usage table | shows which tables and resources send the most data | review it after every new data source

Warning: A workspace daily cap stops collecting billable data for the rest of the day once the cap is reached. It protects the budget, but it blinds you exactly when an incident floods the logs. Use it only as a safety net set well above normal volume, and alert on rising ingestion instead.

6. Friday's answer for Nusantara Retail

With all three pipes feeding log-nusa, the Monday meeting changed. Instead of three screens and three theories, the team opened one workspace and asked questions in order, from symptom to cause:

1. AppRequests showed the p95 of checkout jumping from about 400 ms to 2.8 seconds at 19:05, while the home page and product list stayed fast. The problem was specific to checkout.
2. AppDependencies showed why: calls to the payment provider's API took 2.4 seconds at p95, while the database and Blob storage calls stayed normal. The application map drew the same picture, with one red line to the payment API.
3. Perf and StorageBlobLogs cleared the other suspects: the order-jobs VM stayed below 50% CPU, and blob latency was flat all evening. Dewi's images and Pak Budi's VM were innocent.
4. Rizky was right. The payment provider had throttled merchants during the evening peak.

The fix is part technical, part conversation: a standard availability test against the payment provider's status endpoint, a log search alert on the p95 of payment dependency calls, sensible timeouts with a friendly retry message for customers, a workbook the whole team can open, and a call with the provider about higher limits before 12.12. Ibu Sari got her answer in twenty minutes instead of a week of arguments — and the same queries will watch Harbolnas.

Pause and think: Your log search alert runs every 5 minutes over the last 5 minutes, but during busy periods Syslog rows arrive up to 4 minutes late. What could go wrong, and which two settings would you change?

Next, Lunch 31 scales governance across the whole company, including the Azure Policy definitions that deploy agents and diagnostic settings automatically.

Field notes from Stefanus

Silence is not the same as health. A query that returns nothing looks exactly like a system with no problems. So after every change to an agent, a data collection rule or a diagnostic setting, I send a known test message with a unique marker, such as a logger line or a test request, and I don't move on until a query finds it. For every source that matters, I also keep one alert that watches for silence: a computer whose last Heartbeat is more than ten minutes old, or a table that has received no rows in the last hour. A threshold alert on data that has stopped arriving can never fire, and nothing on your screen tells you so. The trap I see most often is a rule that everyone trusts, faithfully evaluating a table that stopped filling long ago.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Azure Monitor Logs overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/logs/data-platform-logs) — workspaces, table plans and their features side by side.
- Microsoft Learn: Install and manage the Azure Monitor Agent (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/agents/azure-monitor-agent-manage) — installation options, identities and how to verify the agent with a Heartbeat query.
- Microsoft Learn: Tutorial: Learn common KQL operators (https://learn.microsoft.com/kusto/query/tutorials/learn-common-operators) — a hands-on tour of the operators in this lunch, with sample data.
- Microsoft Learn: Enable OpenTelemetry in Application Insights (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/app/opentelemetry-enable) — the current distros and how to connect an app with a connection string.

quiz.q: Pak Budi installed the Azure Monitor Agent on a new Linux VM an hour ago. The extension shows Provisioning succeeded, but the Heartbeat table has no rows for that VM. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.a: The VM has no data collection rule associated (or no managed identity for the agent to authenticate with). Why: the agent collects nothing until a DCR association tells it what to collect and where to send it.

quiz.q: The security team needs three years of firewall logs for audits and queries them a few times a year. Which table plan fits, and what's the trade-off?
quiz.a: Auxiliary (or Basic), with total retention set to three years. Why: ingestion is far cheaper; in return queries are slower, are charged per GB scanned, and can't drive standard alerts — fine for rare audit questions.

quiz.q: Dewi writes AppRequests | summarize avg(DurationMs) and sees 620 ms, yet customers complain about four-second checkouts. What should she change?
quiz.a: Filter to the checkout operation and the right time range, then use percentiles per time bucket — for example percentile(DurationMs, 95) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m). Why: an average over everything hides the slow tail that customers actually feel.

quiz.q: A join of failed requests with exceptions on OperationId returns fewer rows than expected. Which detail of KQL explains it?
quiz.a: Without kind=, a KQL join is innerunique, which keeps only one left-side row per key, and inner joins drop requests that have no exception at all. Use kind=leftouter (or kind=inner) on purpose. Why: the default join kind deduplicates the left side.

quiz.q: Nusantara Retail wants to know from outside the company network whether customers in Jakarta, Singapore and Tokyo can reach the storefront. Which feature fits, and which kind should you create?
quiz.a: An Application Insights availability test of the standard kind, running from several locations (five or more is recommended), with an alert when multiple locations fail. Why: URL ping tests were retired in September 2026, and standard tests also check TLS certificates, verbs and headers.

takeaways: Design the workspace first — fewest workspaces that satisfy residency and ownership, resource-context access, the right retention, and the right table plan per table.

Use the right pipe: diagnostic settings for platform logs, the Azure Monitor Agent plus a data collection rule (associated, with a managed identity) for guest data, and Application Insights for application telemetry.
KQL is a pipeline: start with the table, filter on time, then filter, summarise, bin and render; choose join kinds deliberately and prefer percentiles for latency.
Application Insights is workspace-based and OpenTelemetry-based: requests, dependencies, exceptions and traces share an operation ID, and standard availability tests watch from outside.
Turn good queries into log search alerts and workbooks — and control cost by collecting less, choosing table plans wisely and watching the Usage table.

lab.title: Why was checkout slow on Friday?
lab.text:
What you'll build

Last Friday Nusantara Retail's checkout took four seconds while every CPU chart looked fine. Dewi blames the product images, Pak Budi the order-jobs VM, Rizky the payment provider. Today you build the evidence room that settles it: one Log Analytics workspace fed by three pipes — the Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule on the VM, a diagnostic setting on Blob storage, and Application Insights on the storefront web app. Then you answer ten graded KQL questions, turn the slow-checkout query into a log search alert, and repair a data collection rule that silently drops warnings.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources and assign roles on them (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install: setup.sh adds the Azure CLI extensions this lab uses (monitor-control-service, application-insights, scheduled-query and log-analytics).
- Optional: an email address you can read during the lab, if you want the alert in your inbox.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings and the lab's resource names:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/30-monitoring-advanced
source ../common/config.sh
source lab.env

- Create the starting point: the workspace log-nusa, the VM vm-nusa-app, the storage account stnusalog<suffix> and the storefront web app — with nothing monitored yet. It takes about 6–10 minutes:

bash setup.sh

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Note: Monitoring data isn't instant. A brand-new agent, rule, diagnostic setting or Application Insights resource usually needs 5–15 minutes before its first rows appear. The tasks are ordered so you can keep working while data starts flowing; Task 6 is where you query it.

Tip: Cloud Shell disconnects after about 20 minutes without typing. If that happens, reconnect and reload the variables:

cd ~/azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/30-monitoring-advanced && source ../common/config.sh && source lab.env
LAW_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show -g "$RG" -n "$LAW" --query id -o tsv)
LAW_GUID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show -g "$RG" -n "$LAW" --query customerId -o tsv)
VM_ID=$(az vm show -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query id -o tsv)
ST_ID=$(az storage account show -g "$RG" -n "$ST" --query id -o tsv)
HOST=$(az webapp show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query defaultHostName -o tsv)
kql() { az monitor log-analytics query --workspace "$LAW_GUID" --analytics-query "$1" --output table; }

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–7 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Tour the evidence room

Start with the empty workspace: where it lives, how long it keeps data, and how to ask it a question from Cloud Shell.

LAW_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name "$LAW" --query id --output tsv)
LAW_GUID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name "$LAW" --query customerId --output tsv)

az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name "$LAW" \
  --query "{name:name, location:location, pricing:sku.name, retentionDays:retentionInDays, workspaceGuid:customerId}" \
  --output yaml

# Plan and retention of a table you'll fill today
az monitor log-analytics workspace table show --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name "$LAW" --name Syslog \
  --query "{table:name, plan:plan || properties.plan, analyticsDays:retentionInDays || properties.retentionInDays, totalDays:totalRetentionInDays || properties.totalRetentionInDays}" \
  --output yaml

# A small helper that runs KQL from Cloud Shell. It needs the workspace GUID, not the name.
kql() { az monitor log-analytics query --workspace "$LAW_GUID" --analytics-query "$1" --output table; }
kql 'print Message = "Selamat siang from log-nusa", Now = now()'

The workspace has two IDs: the Azure resource ID (LAW_ID), which you use to send data to it, and the workspace GUID (LAW_GUID, called Workspace ID in the portal), which you use to query it.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open log-nusa › Settings › Tables to see every table's plan and retention, then Logs. Switch the editor from Simple mode to KQL mode — you'll use KQL mode for the rest of the lab.

Checkpoint: retentionDays: 30, the Syslog table on the Analytics plan with 30 days of analytics retention, and one row with your greeting and the current time.

Task 2 · Give the VM an identity and the Azure Monitor Agent

The Azure Monitor Agent signs in to Azure Monitor with the VM's managed identity — no keys or workspace secrets. Give the VM a system-assigned identity, then install the agent as a VM extension:

VM_ID=$(az vm show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$VM" --query id --output tsv)

az vm identity assign --resource-group "$RG" --name "$VM" --output none

az vm extension set \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --vm-name "$VM" \
  --name AzureMonitorLinuxAgent \
  --publisher Microsoft.Azure.Monitor \
  --enable-auto-upgrade true \
  --output none

az vm show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$VM" --query identity.type --output tsv
az vm extension list --resource-group "$RG" --vm-name "$VM" \
  --query "[].{name:name, version:typeHandlerVersion, state:provisioningState, autoUpgrade:enableAutomaticUpgrade}" \
  --output table

Now ask the workspace whether the agent reports anything:

kql 'Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | summarize count() by Computer'

Nothing. That's expected: the agent doesn't collect anything until a data collection rule tells it what to collect and where to send it. That's Task 3.

Tip: Prefer the portal? VM › Settings › Identity › System assigned: On. Then VM › Settings › Extensions + applications › Add › Azure Monitor Agent for Linux. (Creating a data collection rule in the portal also installs the agent for you.)

Checkpoint: the identity type is SystemAssigned, AzureMonitorLinuxAgent shows Succeeded with auto-upgrade on, and the Heartbeat query returns no rows.

Task 3 · Tell the agent what to collect: a data collection rule

Read the rule first — it's short:

cat dcr-linux-nusa.json

Part | What it says
dataSources.syslog | collect Syslog from the auth, authpriv, cron, daemon, syslog and user facilities, at Warning and above
dataSources.performanceCounters | sample CPU, memory, disk and network counters every 60 seconds
destinations.logAnalytics | one destination named la-nusa: the workspace whose resource ID replaces __WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID__
dataFlows | send the Syslog and Perf streams to la-nusa (they land in the Syslog and Perf tables)

Fill in your workspace, create the rule, and associate it with the VM:

mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR"
sed "s|__WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID__|${LAW_ID}|" dcr-linux-nusa.json > "$OUT_DIR/dcr.json"

az monitor data-collection rule create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --name "$DCR" \
  --rule-file "$OUT_DIR/dcr.json" \
  --output none
DCR_ID=$(az monitor data-collection rule show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$DCR" --query id --output tsv)

az monitor data-collection rule association create \
  --name "$DCR_ASSOC" \
  --rule-id "$DCR_ID" \
  --resource "$VM_ID" \
  --output none

az monitor data-collection rule association list --resource "$VM_ID" \
  --query "[].{association:name, rule:dataCollectionRuleId || properties.dataCollectionRuleId}" --output table

The rule must be in the same region as the workspace it sends to; here everything is in $LOCATION. The association is what connects one machine to one rule — in production, Azure Policy creates associations for every new VM (Lunch 31).

Now give the order-jobs server something to say. Run Command writes three messages to Syslog at three severities:

az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "logger -p user.warning -t nusa-orders 'Order batch 4471 retry 3/5: payment API slow'; logger -p user.info -t nusa-orders 'Order batch 4471 started'; logger -p user.err -t nusa-orders 'Order batch 4470 failed after 5 retries'" \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

Which of the three should reach the workspace? You'll check in Task 6. Heartbeats should start within about 5–10 minutes; carry on with Task 4 meanwhile.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Monitor › Settings › Data Collection Rules › Create. On Resources add vm-nusa-app; on Collect and deliver add Linux Syslog (minimum log level LOG_WARNING) and Performance Counters, each with log-nusa as the destination. Open the finished rule's JSON View and compare it with the file.

Checkpoint: the association list shows dcra-vm-nusa-app pointing at .../dataCollectionRules/dcr-linux-nusa, and Run Command returns without errors.

Task 4 · Platform logs: a diagnostic setting for Blob storage

Dewi's product images live in Blob storage. Who reads them, how fast, and which reads fail? The storage service writes those resource logs only if you route them somewhere. For storage, the setting goes on the blob service (.../blobServices/default), not on the storage account itself:

ST_ID=$(az storage account show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$ST" --query id --output tsv)

# Which log categories does the blob service offer?
az monitor diagnostic-settings categories list --resource "$ST_ID/blobServices/default" \
  --query "(value || @)[].{category:name, type:categoryType}" --output table

az monitor diagnostic-settings create \
  --name "$DIAG" \
  --resource "$ST_ID/blobServices/default" \
  --workspace "$LAW_ID" \
  --logs '[{"categoryGroup":"allLogs","enabled":true}]' \
  --output none

az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource "$ST_ID/blobServices/default" \
  --query "(value || @)[].{name:name, workspace:workspaceId, logs:logs[].categoryGroup}" --output yaml

- categoryGroup: allLogs means "every log category, including any added later" — here StorageRead, StorageWrite and StorageDelete. The audit group is the smaller alternative.
- Storage logs land in the resource-specific table StorageBlobLogs.
- A diagnostic setting outlives its resource. That's why cleanup.sh deletes it explicitly.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage account › Monitoring › Diagnostic settings › select blob › Add diagnostic setting. Tick allLogs and Send to Log Analytics workspace › log-nusa.

Checkpoint: one setting named diag-blob-to-log-nusa whose workspace ends in /workspaces/log-nusa and whose logs list allLogs.

Task 5 · Application Insights for the storefront

The storefront in app/app.py contains no monitoring code at all. You'll turn on autoinstrumentation: App Service loads Microsoft's OpenTelemetry-based agent into the Python process and sends requests, exceptions and logged warnings to a workspace-based Application Insights resource.

az monitor app-insights component create \
  --app "$APPI" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --workspace "$LAW_ID" \
  --application-type web \
  --output none
APPI_ID=$(az monitor app-insights component show --app "$APPI" --resource-group "$RG" --query id --output tsv)
CONN=$(az monitor app-insights component show --app "$APPI" --resource-group "$RG" --query connectionString --output tsv)

az webapp config appsettings set --resource-group "$RG" --name "$APP" \
  --settings "APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING=$CONN" \
             "ApplicationInsightsAgent_EXTENSION_VERSION=~3" \
             "OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=nusa-storefront" \
  --output none

App setting | Why
APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING | where to send telemetry (it identifies appi-nusa-shop)
ApplicationInsightsAgent_EXTENSION_VERSION=~3 | turns on the App Service-managed agent on Linux
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME | a standard OpenTelemetry setting: the name shown on the application map and in AppRoleName

Changing app settings restarts the app. Next, watch the storefront from outside with a standard availability test that calls /health every 5 minutes from five locations: Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, Australia and the US West Coast.

HOST=$(az webapp show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$APP" --query defaultHostName --output tsv)

az monitor app-insights web-test create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$WEBTEST" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --web-test-kind standard \
  --defined-web-test-name "$WEBTEST" \
  --synthetic-monitor-id "$WEBTEST" \
  --enabled true \
  --frequency 300 \
  --timeout 30 \
  --retry-enabled true \
  --locations Id=apac-sg-sin-azr \
  --locations Id=apac-hk-hkn-azr \
  --locations Id=apac-jp-kaw-edge \
  --locations Id=emea-au-syd-edge \
  --locations Id=us-ca-sjc-azr \
  --http-verb GET \
  --request-url "https://$HOST/health" \
  --expected-status-code 200 \
  --tags "hidden-link:$APPI_ID=Resource" \
  --output none

The hidden-link tag is what attaches the test to appi-nusa-shop, so its results appear under Availability and in the AppAvailabilityResults table. Standard tests are billed per run, so this lab keeps the frequency at 5 minutes.

Finally, play Friday evening. traffic.sh sends shoppers to the storefront and reads and writes product images; run it in the background for 25 minutes:

nohup bash traffic.sh 25 > "$OUT_DIR/traffic.log" 2>&1 &
sleep 60; tail -n 3 "$OUT_DIR/traffic.log"

Tip: Prefer the portal? Web app › Monitoring › Application Insights › Turn on Application Insights sets the same app settings for you. For the test: appi-nusa-shop › Investigate › Availability › Add Standard test.

Checkpoint: the traffic log shows rounds with some slow and a few failed checkouts, and az monitor app-insights web-test list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[].name" --output tsv prints avail-nusa-health. If the log mentions failed storage calls, your new role assignment is still propagating — keep going.

Task 6 · Ten KQL questions

Give the pipes about ten minutes after Task 5, then check what has arrived:

kql 'union isfuzzy=true withsource=SourceTable Heartbeat, Syslog, Perf, StorageBlobLogs, AppRequests, AppTraces, AppExceptions, AppAvailabilityResults
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable'

The portal is the comfortable place for this task: log-nusa › Logs, KQL mode, time range Set in query. Every solution below also works in Cloud Shell as kql '<query>' (charts are portal-only; the CLI prints the rows).

Grading: = 1 point, = 2 points, = 3 points — 20 points in total. Write your query, run it, and only then open the solution. Fourteen points or more and you're ready for on-call.

1. Is the agent alive? Which computers send heartbeats through the Azure Monitor Agent, and when did each last check in?

Solution 1

Heartbeat
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Category == "Azure Monitor Agent"
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Heartbeats = count() by Computer, OSType, Version

Expect one row for vm-nusa-app with roughly one heartbeat per minute since the association. Heartbeat is free to ingest.

2. What did the order-jobs server warn about? List the Syslog warnings of the last four hours, newest first.

Solution 2

Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(4h)
| where SeverityLevel =~ "warning"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Your Order batch 4471 retry 3/5 message from nusa-orders is there. Remove the severity filter and you'll also find the err message — but never the info one: the DCR collects Warning and above, so the agent dropped it at the source.

3. What happened to the product images? Count blob operations by operation name, result and authentication type.

Solution 3

StorageBlobLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(4h)
| summarize Requests = count() by OperationName, StatusText, AuthenticationType
| sort by Requests desc

You'll see PutBlob, ListBlobs and GetBlob with Success over OAuth, plus GetBlob with BlobNotFound — the 12.12 banner that doesn't exist. Rows with AuthorizationPermissionMismatch come from the minutes before your role assignment applied.

4. Is Pak Budi's VM busy? Chart the average CPU of each computer in 5-minute buckets for the last hour.

Solution 4

Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ObjectName == "Processor" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| summarize AvgCpu = avg(CounterValue) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), Computer
| render timechart

A flat, low line: the VM is innocent.

5. How much memory is left? Show only the newest Available MBytes Memory sample for each computer.

Solution 5

Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ObjectName == "Memory" and CounterName == "Available MBytes Memory"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, CounterValue) by Computer
| project Computer, LastSample = TimeGenerated, AvailableMB = CounterValue

arg_max(TimeGenerated, CounterValue) keeps the whole latest row per computer instead of averaging.

6. Which operations fail? For each request name, show the number of requests, failures and the failure percentage, worst first.

Solution 6

AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize Requests = count(), Failed = countif(Success == false) by Name
| extend FailedPct = round(100.0 * Failed / Requests, 1)
| sort by FailedPct desc

POST /checkout fails about 7% of the time; GET /products, GET / and the availability test's GET /health don't fail at all.

7. What did the code say? Count the warnings that mention the payment gateway in 5-minute buckets, as a column chart.

Solution 7

AppTraces
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where SeverityLevel == 2 and Message has "Payment gateway"
| summarize Warnings = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| render columnchart

In AppTraces, SeverityLevel 2 means Warning. These rows come from Python's logging module — autoinstrumentation collects the root logger.

8. The chart for Ibu Sari. Plot the median and the 95th-percentile duration of checkout requests in 5-minute buckets.

Solution 8

AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Name has "checkout"
| summarize p50 = percentile(DurationMs, 50), p95 = percentile(DurationMs, 95) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| render timechart

The median stays around 200–300 ms while the p95 sits near 2,500–3,000 ms: most customers are fine, and one in five waits for the payment provider. An average would have hidden that.

9. Why did those checkouts fail? List the failed requests of the last hour with the exception type and message of the same operation. Keep failed requests that have no exception.

Solution 9

AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) and Success == false
| project TimeGenerated, OperationId, Name, ResultCode, DurationMs
| join kind=leftouter (
    AppExceptions
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, ExceptionType, OuterMessage) by OperationId
  ) on OperationId
| project TimeGenerated, Name, ResultCode, DurationMs, ExceptionType, OuterMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Every failure is a POST /checkout with result code 500 after about three seconds, and the exception says the payment provider didn't answer. kind=leftouter keeps requests without an exception, and the summarize on the right side keeps one exception per operation so rows don't multiply. Rizky was right.

10. What does this evidence cost? Show the billable megabytes ingested per table over the last day, largest first, as a pie chart.

Solution 10

Usage
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where IsBillable == true
| summarize BillableMB = round(sum(Quantity), 2) by DataType
| sort by BillableMB desc
| render piechart

Quantity is in MB. Heartbeat doesn't appear because it's free. Usage is written in batches, so early in the lab it may still be empty — run it again at the end.

Checkpoint: questions 1, 6 and 8 return rows. If a table is still empty, wait a few minutes and use the Troubleshooting table.

Task 7 · From query to alert

Question 8 found the problem; now make sure you hear about it next time. A log search alert runs a query on a schedule. If you want an email, create an action group first (skip this block otherwise):

export ALERT_EMAIL="you@example.com"     # change this to your own address
az monitor action-group create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$AG" \
  --short-name nusaoncall \
  --action email oncall-email "$ALERT_EMAIL" usecommonalertschema \
  --output none
AG_ID=$(az monitor action-group show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AG" --query id --output tsv)

Create the rule. If you skipped the action group, leave out the --action-groups line:

az monitor scheduled-query create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$ALERT" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --scopes "$LAW_ID" \
  --condition "count 'SlowCheckout' > 3 at least 1 violations out of 1 aggregated points" \
  --condition-query SlowCheckout="AppRequests | where Name has 'checkout' and DurationMs > 1000" \
  --window-size 10m \
  --evaluation-frequency 5m \
  --severity 3 \
  --description "More than 3 checkouts slower than 1 second in 10 minutes" \
  --action-groups "$AG_ID" \
  --output none

az monitor scheduled-query show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$ALERT" \
  --query "{enabled:enabled, every:evaluationFrequency, window:windowSize, query:criteria.allOf[0].query, operator:criteria.allOf[0].operator, threshold:criteria.allOf[0].threshold}" \
  --output yaml

Part | Meaning
--condition-query SlowCheckout="…" | the query, under a placeholder name; it returns the slow checkouts, not a verdict
--condition "count 'SlowCheckout' > 3 …" | count the rows the query returns and fire when there are more than 3
--window-size 10m | each run looks at the last 10 minutes: twice the frequency, so rows that arrive late are still counted
--evaluation-frequency 5m | run every 5 minutes (1-minute rules cost more)
--scopes "$LAW_ID" | the workspace that holds AppRequests

The alert needs slow checkouts to count. If traffic.sh has finished (tail -n 2 "$OUT_DIR/traffic.log" says Done), start it again:

nohup bash traffic.sh 15 > "$OUT_DIR/traffic.log" 2>&1 &

The alert fires within about 5–15 minutes. Watch Monitor › Alerts in the portal, filtered on your resource group.

Optional — a workbook for the whole team (portal, about 5 minutes): log-nusa › Workbooks › New. Add › Add query, paste solution 8 and choose Time chart; add a second query with solution 6 as a Grid. Select Done editing, then Save it as Checkout health in your lab resource group. That's the page Ibu Sari can open before 12.12.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Run solution 8 without the render line in Logs, then select New alert rule. The query comes with it: set Measure to Table rows, Aggregation granularity to 10 minutes, the threshold to 3 and the frequency to 5 minutes.

Checkpoint: the rule shows enabled: true, every: PT5M, window: PT10M and threshold: 3.0, and a fired alert-slow-checkout alert (Sev 3) appears under Monitor › Alerts — plus an email if you created the action group.

Break it and fix it

Rizky trimmed the data collection rule "to cut the log bill". Apply his version:

sed 's/"Warning", //' "$OUT_DIR/dcr.json" > "$OUT_DIR/dcr-rizky.json"
grep logLevels "$OUT_DIR/dcr-rizky.json"
az monitor data-collection rule create --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --name "$DCR" \
  --rule-file "$OUT_DIR/dcr-rizky.json" --output none

Wait about five minutes for the agent to pick up the change, then let the order-jobs server report two problems with the marker rizkytest:

az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "logger -p user.warning -t nusa-orders 'Payment API slow again (rizkytest)'; logger -p user.err -t nusa-orders 'Order batch 4480 failed (rizkytest)'" \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

Symptom: ten minutes later, only one of the two messages is in the workspace, and bash verify.sh fails a check.

kql 'Syslog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30m) | where SyslogMessage has "rizkytest" | project TimeGenerated, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage'

Hint: what's missing, and how do you fix it?

The error arrived; the warning didn't. Rizky's rule lists only Error, Critical, Alert and Emergency, so the agent now drops every warning on the VM before it's sent — including the "payment API slow" warnings that would have explained Friday. Filtering at the source is the right way to save money, but only for data nobody needs.

Re-create the rule from the original file, which includes Warning:

az monitor data-collection rule create --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --name "$DCR" \
  --rule-file "$OUT_DIR/dcr.json" --output none

Wait about five minutes, run the logger command again with the marker rizkyfixed, and query for it ten minutes later: both severities arrive. The warning you sent during the break is gone for good — the agent doesn't backfill what a rule filtered out.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The last section counts rows per table as notes: if a table is still empty, wait a few minutes and run the script again.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes, in order: the diagnostic setting on the blob service (diagnostic settings can outlive their resource), your Storage Blob Data Contributor role assignment, the workspace log-nusa — permanently, instead of keeping it soft-deleted for 14 days — and then resource group rg-lunch30-<suffix> with everything else in it: the VM and its network resources, the storage account, the App Service plan and web app, Application Insights with its availability test, the data collection rule, the alert rule and the action group. It also removes the local folder $HOME/lab30-out. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

If you created a subscription-level diagnostic setting in the stretch goals, delete it too — it isn't in the resource group.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
An az monitor data-collection, app-insights, scheduled-query or log-analytics query command asks to install an extension, or says it isn't recognized | the CLI extension isn't installed in this Cloud Shell | run bash setup.sh again, or az extension add --name monitor-control-service (and application-insights, scheduled-query, log-analytics)
setup.sh fails on the App Service plan with a quota error | your subscription has no quota for Basic plans in this region | run export LAB30_APP_SKU=F1 (Free) or choose another LOCATION, then source lab.env and bash setup.sh again
No Heartbeat rows 15 minutes after Task 3 | no managed identity, no association, the agent can't reach Azure Monitor, or the rule and workspace are in different regions | re-run the Task 2 and Task 3 checks; the VM needs its public IP for outbound HTTPS; recreate the rule in the workspace's region
Heartbeat rows arrive but no Syslog warnings | the rule doesn't include Warning, or the message was sent before the rule applied | grep logLevels "$OUT_DIR/dcr.json"; send a new warning with Task 3's logger command and wait 10 minutes
StorageBlobLogs stays empty | the diagnostic setting is on the storage account instead of .../blobServices/default, or no blob traffic yet | re-run Task 4 exactly; check $OUT_DIR/traffic.log for storage rounds
traffic.sh reports failed storage rounds for more than 10 minutes | the role assignment from setup.sh is missing | az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" --assignee-principal-type User --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" --scope "$ST_ID"
No AppRequests rows 15 minutes after Task 5 | the app settings are missing or misspelled, or the app hasn't restarted | check them with az webapp config appsettings list --resource-group "$RG" --name "$APP" --output table; az webapp restart --resource-group "$RG" --name "$APP"; make sure traffic.sh is still running
az monitor log-analytics query says the workspace wasn't found | you passed the workspace name or resource ID | use the GUID: $LAW_GUID (the Workspace ID in the portal)
The alert rule can't be created: Failed to resolve table or column expression named 'AppRequests' | Application Insights hasn't sent its first data yet | wait until question 6 returns rows, then run the command again (or add --skip-query-validation true)
The alert hasn't fired after 15 minutes | not enough slow checkouts in a 10-minute window | check that traffic.sh is running (tail "$OUT_DIR/traffic.log"); start it again with nohup bash traffic.sh 15 > "$OUT_DIR/traffic.log" 2>&1 &
